Questions 1-4

Reading Passage 1 has eight sections, A-H.

Which section contains the following information?

Questions 5-8

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Packaging made from fungi

Concern about plastic waste has led [5] to try making packaging from mycelium, the thread-like part of a mushroom. There are some problems with this material. For example, it can take in [6] from the air, so it cannot be used for many types of food. To make the packaging, fungal threads are combined with farm waste such as the [7] of hemp plants and left to grow in moulds. Compared with polystyrene, it uses much less [8] to produce, and it breaks down quickly in soil.

Questions 14-20

Reading Passage 2 has seven paragraphs, A-G.

Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.

List of Headings
i   An impressive result in a long-distance trial
ii   Poor marketing causes a decline in sales
iii   The strengths and weaknesses of an early technology
iv   A question for the present day
v   Technical improvements lead to growing sales
vi   An elegant vehicle wins public approval
vii   Owners are disappointed by the car's performance
viii   A cheaper rival takes over the market

Questions 24-26

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
The Detroit Electric

In a well-known test, a Detroit Electric reportedly travelled [24] miles without needing to be recharged. However, sales declined during the 1920s, and when the company closed in [25], most of its customers were [26] people, many of whom were elderly.

groups.instruction:
Questions 31-35

Complete the summary using the list of phrases, A-I, below.

Write the correct letter, A-I, in boxes 31-35 on your answer sheet.

A   frequent tests
B   clear guidance
C   group rewards
D   unfamiliar problems
E   weak foundations
F   a full explanation
G   extra homework
H   a deeper understanding
I   faster progress
groups.content:
Research into productive failure

Professor Nina Vogel found that students who struggled with a problem before being taught the method developed [31] of the ideas involved. The advantage was most obvious when students were asked to solve [32]. However, struggling only helped if it was followed by [33] from the teacher. Vogel also warns that the approach may not suit students with [34] in basic skills, and that teachers should give [35] about what students should do while they are struggling.

groups.instruction:
Questions 36-40

Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 36-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: G Section G: alternatives 'make use of materials that would otherwise be wasted', and ' Some bioplastics are made from the waste left over after sugar has been extracted from sugarcane '. Section E mentions farm waste, but explains how fungal packaging is grown, not industrial by-products.
Answer: D Section D: ' Mushroom-based packaging is already being produced in the United States, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom '.
Answer: C Section C: ' the oil and gas from which most plastics are made are cheap and available in enormous quantities '.
Answer: F Section F: Berg says ' until they have been used successfully on a large scale... it will be hard to regard them as a genuine replacement for plastic '.
Answer: designers Section D: 'Growing concern about plastic waste has encouraged designers to experiment with mycelium'.
Answer: water Section E: 'The material can absorb water from its surroundings, which makes it unsuitable for many foods'.
Answer: husks Section E: 'farm waste such as the husks of hemp plants is mixed with fungal threads'.
Answer: energy Section E: 'Unlike polystyrene, it requires very little energy to make'.
Answer: C (Sarah Quinn) Section G: Quinn notes that 'the benefits are not always as clear as they seem', and if raw materials are shipped far, ' much of the environmental advantage may be lost '.
Answer: A (Martin Hale) Section C: ' Finding another material that offers all of those benefits at the same time is going to be extremely difficult. '
Answer: B (Lena Berg) Section F: Berg reports a sharp rise in orders for paper packaging, ' with customers' worries about plastic pollution as the main driving force '.
Answer: D (Siddiqui and Dunn) Section H: alternatives have not achieved widespread use; ' They are generally more expensive than conventional plastic '.
Answer: A (Martin Hale) Section B: ' The problem is the sheer quantity of plastic that we use once and then throw away. It is the scale that makes it so damaging.'
Answer: iii Paragraph A lists the attractions of electric cars ('quiet... no fumes... no hand crank') and their 'serious weaknesses' (heavy batteries, limited range).
Answer: viii Mass production made the Model T cheap, petrol became cheap, and ' Within a few years, petrol cars dominated the market. '
Answer: vi The cars had 'elegant, closed bodies', and ' Newspapers and magazines praised the car for its quietness and cleanliness'.
Answer: v The company improved the car (Edison battery, speed, range), and ' Orders rose steadily '.
Answer: vii For many owners, ' the reality was less satisfactory than the advertising had suggested ': no charging stations, costly batteries, reduced range in winter.
Answer: i 'In one widely reported test, a Detroit Electric was said to have travelled 211 miles on a single charge '.
Answer: iv As electric vehicles return, ' it is tempting to wonder how different the history of transport might have been ', a question relevant today.

text.en: Their popularity did not last long.
They were more dangerous to drive.
Few companies were willing to make them.
They could not be used on the new roads.

questions.explanation: Answer: A Paragraph B opens: ' The advantage did not last. ' Within a few years petrol cars dominated. The hand crank on petrol cars was the dangerous feature (B).

text.en: copied the design of an existing electric car.
moved his factory to a new city.
made use of his experience in a previous business.
asked Henry Ford for financial support.

questions.explanation: Answer: C Anderson had made horse-drawn carriages, and ' drew heavily on his experience of carriage-making '. Ford's wife owned a car (D is not stated).

text.en: increased their top speed to compete with petrol cars.
offered a longer-lasting battery at an additional cost.
built its own network of charging stations.
replaced the lever with a steering wheel.

questions.explanation: Answer: B ' For an extra charge, customers could choose a battery developed by the inventor Thomas Edison ', which lasted much longer. The charging network never appeared (C).
Answer: 211 Paragraph F: the car 'was said to have travelled 211 miles on a single charge'. 80 miles was the normal range (trap).
Answer: 1939 Paragraph G: 'by the time the company finally closed in 1939 '.
Answer: wealthy Paragraph G: 'its cars were bought almost entirely by wealthy customers, many of them elderly people'.

text.en: how few students enjoy mathematics.
how students respond when they are not taught a method first.
how difficult the maths curriculum has become.
how some students disturb the learning of others.

questions.explanation: Answer: B ' I have deliberately not shown them any method. ' The paragraph then describes the students' different reactions: drawing charts, arguing, giving up, inventing their own method.

text.en: It is widely liked.
It works best for the most able students.
It is difficult for teachers to assess.
It is used more in some countries than others.

questions.explanation: Answer: A The approach ' is popular with almost everyone involved ': students, parents and teachers. It is described as 'easy to assess' (C).

text.en: students who are afraid of making mistakes
students who need more time to practise
students who lack real understanding of what they have learned
students who ignore the advice of their teachers

questions.explanation: Answer: C Like the driver who panics in an unexpected situation, ' students who have only practised a method may produce correct answers without having any real understanding '.

text.en: problems that students choose for themselves
tests that measure how much students remember
challenges that slow learning down but make it last longer
tasks that are too hard for most students to complete

questions.explanation: Answer: C ' tasks which make learning feel slower and harder at the time ... often lead to knowledge that lasts much longer'.

Answer: H (a deeper understanding) 'the students who had struggled first showed a deeper understanding of the underlying ideas'. On standard questions both groups did similarly, so not 'faster progress' (I).
Answer: D (unfamiliar problems) 'they were far more successful when asked to solve unfamiliar problems '.
Answer: F (a full explanation) 'The benefits appeared only when the period of struggle was followed by a full explanation from the teacher'.
Answer: E (weak foundations) 'the approach may be less suitable for students with weak foundations in basic skills'.
Answer: B (clear guidance) 'teachers need to give clear guidance about what students are expected to do while they struggle'.
Answer: NO Paragraph 6: if the idea is true, then ' removing every obstacle from students' paths may be doing them a disservice '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer discusses Vogel's research and warnings, but says nothing about other teachers trying and abandoning the approach.
Answer: YES Paragraph 9: students are 'no longer simply copying' the method; ' They recognise it as a solution to a problem they have been wrestling with '.
Answer: NO Paragraph 10: ' we have become too anxious to protect students from difficulty ', depriving them of the chance to think for themselves.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer talks about curiosity in the writer's own class but gives no information about students' later choices of university subject.
